Leader development
A review of more than a century's studies on psychological aspects of leadership reveals a notable absence of comprehensive and
methodical discussion and research on developmental psychological aspects of leaders (Avolio, 1999, 2005; Avolio & Gibbons, 1988;
Day, Zaccaro, & Halpin, 2004; Klonsky,1983; Kuhnert & Lewis,1987; London, 2002; McCauley, & Van Velsor, 2004; Popper & Mayseless,
2002; Zacharatos, Barling, & Kelloway, 2000).
Most evidence on the development of leaders has been supplied by historians who studied the lives of outstanding leaders (e.g.,
Bullock,1991; Burns,1956). Characteristically, these studies (1) focus on exceptional leaders who are of great interest to historians, and
(2) analyze their development mainly from a psychoanalytic viewpoint (Burns, 1978). Such studies are clearly limited with regard to
the possibility of generalization. This criticism is often directed at psychoanalytical research in general (Meadow, 1996), but it is even
more relevant in the case of historical studies of outstanding (usually political) personages (Burns,1978). They do not necessarily shed
light on leaders of local communities, organizational units, social frameworks, and the like, namely those who might be described as
“leaders in everyday life.”

3.3. Discussion
Study 1 provides causal evidence that perceiving one’s future as
limited leads to an increase in conﬁrmatory information processing.

Adding representational pictures (RPs) to text-based items has been shown to improve students’ test perfor-
mance. Focusing on potential explanations for this multimedia eﬀect in testing, we propose two functions of RPs in
testing, namely, (1) a cognitive facilitation function and (2) a motivational function. We found empirical support for
both functions in this computer-based classroom experiment with N = 410 ﬁfth and sixth graders. All students
answered 36 manipulated science items that either contained (text-picture) or did not contain (text-only) an RP
that visualized the text information in the item stem. Each student worked on both item types, following a
rotated within-subject design. We measured students’ (a) solution success, (b) time on task (TOT), and identiﬁed

history, individuals perceived as wise, such as Socrates, Confucius, Buddha, and Jesus, have also been considered great leaders.
Since the industrial revolution, with the advent of the modern economy and globalization, leadership has more often been
linked to effectiveness and efﬁciency in promoting organizational performance and proﬁts (Nahavandi, 2000), and is rarely
considered in relation to wisdom (Srivastva & Cooperrider, 1998) which has its aim at the promotion of good lives for all (Baltes &
Staudinger, 1993; Kekes, 1983; Sternberg, 1998; Yang, 2001, 2008a, 2008b). As a result of such emphasis on organizational
efﬁciency and proﬁts, business researchers generally disregard wisdom as an important factor in outstanding leadership (Beyer &
Niño, 1998; Khandwalla, 1998). Until recently, wisdom has not been mentioned in scholarly discussions of leadership, nor has it
